title: Every time you rehearse a thought, worry, catastrophize, replay an ar...
description: Every time you rehearse a thought, worry, catastrophize, replay an argument, you’re not just “feeling stressed.” Instead, you’re strengthening a circuit.  Hebb's Law says that neurons that fire together wire together. Under chronic stress, the pathways for rumination and threat-scanning get thicker and faster, while the pathways your prefrontal cortex uses for focus and recall get less traffic and start to weaken.  That’s brain fog.  The chemical signals get the headlines, but they’re not the whole story, they’re part of what drives the deeper structural change. And structure is what you can actually go after. Your mind built that pattern one repeated thought at a time, which means your mind can build a different one. This is where self-brain surgery comes in. The fourth commandment of self-brain surgery is I must believe that my mind is in charge of my brain.  The fifth commandment of self-brain surgery is I must believe that self-brain surgery is not a metaphor, it is the mechanism of transforming my life.  Every surgeon operates with intention, not by accident, and so do you. When the fog hits, you don’t just wait for the feeling to pass, you interrupt the circuit. You catch the automatic thought (see II Corinthians 10:5). The third commandment of self-brain surgery is I must believe that most of my automatic thoughts are untrue, so you deliberately rehearse a different pathway on purpose. You preach a verse until your mind rehearses truth instead of noise.  Isaiah 26:3: “You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you.”  Do that consistently, day after day, and you are rebuilding the wiring. Friend, brain fog is not who you are. It’s a circuit you built without meaning to, which means it’s a circuit you can rebuild on purpose.  Also check with your doctor- this can also come from medical issues! title: Feelings are not facts, they are chemical events in your brain.  That...
description: Feelings are not facts, they are chemical events in your brain.  That's the second commandment of self-brain surgery. And it's a game-changer for your life.  Feelings come on quickly, with a rush of physiological signals like racing heartbeat, quick and breath, and the hair on the back of your neck standing up. This is your brain's attempt to make sense of your environment, or out of something you're just thinking about, remembering, or worried about. Your brain doesn't know the difference between something that's actively happening and something you're just imagining. Think about it: when you feel something like a racing pulse, what makes it anxiety versus anticipation? What makes it fear instead of excitement? The answer is that we tell ourselves a story about the meaning behind how we feel. And then the more we focus on that story from the same perspective, the more automatically our brain associates future times when we feel the same physiological events with the same story. But it's not a fact until it's true. And neuroscience research teaches us that an alarming percentage of the automatic thoughts and feelings we have are not true. If you can develop a system of pausing for a moment to give the slower but much more analytical parts of your brain to come online, they will help you interpret what you're feeling and tell yourself a truer story about what's really going on. The Bible calls this "taking every thought captive," II Corinthians 10:5. This one move will make a bigger difference in your quality of life than just about anything else you can do. title: Replay Loop Your brain doesn’t know what time it is. Every time you r...
description: Replay Loop Your brain doesn’t know what time it is. Every time you replay that conversation from last year, that mistake from last month, that moment you wish you could take back from yesterday, your brain treats it like it’s happening right now. Same stress chemicals. Same alarm bells. You’re not remembering it. You’re reliving it, on a loop you built yourself. That's because of two things: your brain doesn't know the difference between what's really happening and what you're just imagining, and neuroplasticity means that your brain automates things that you think about and turns them into programs that it runs without you having to think about them next time.  So, the more you rehearse something from the past or something you're just imagining, the more your brain builds out a reality as if that thing is still here right now. The ninth Commandment of self brain surgery is, "I must believe that what I'm doing I'm getting better at." That means if you're doing things with your mind that are making your brain better at living in the past or worrying about imaginary outcomes, you're getting better at feeling worse. So knock it off. Here’s the shift: you can’t edit the past, but you can stop rehearsing it. Every replay is a rehearsal, and your brain gets better at whatever you rehearse. Let's make neuroplasticity work for us and not against us. We call that self-brain surgery. It's not easy at first, it's hard and holy work. But remember, you get better at whatever you repeatedly do  Philippians 3:13 says it like this: forget what lies behind and strain towards what lies ahead. Not denying it happened, but refusing to keep performing it. There's better stuff in the future, but not if you keep building a brain that lives in the past. There’s a concept in physics called the observer effect. It says that the act of observing a system doesn’t just measure it, it changes it.  The system behaves differently once something is paying attention to it. Watching isn’t neutral. Watching is an intervention. Your brain works the same way.  When you notice your own thought instead of just being swept along by it, “there’s the panic again,” “there’s the excuse again,” “there’s the quit talking again,” you’re not just watching a pattern anymore.  You’re interrupting it. The noticing itself starts to change the circuit. Attention isn’t passive. Attention is surgery. Beholding, watching rightly, is the mechanism of transformation. Not effort alone. Not willpower alone. Attention, aimed at truth, changes what you become. That’s not a coincidence. title: I'm a brain surgeon, and I'm gonna tell you the truth: You can’t be a...
description: I'm a brain surgeon, and I'm gonna tell you the truth: You can’t be anxious and grateful at the same time. Your brain literally can’t run both. Now, you might feel like you can do both at once. What’s actually happening is your brain is toggling between them so fast it feels simultaneous, like a flicker that looks like it’s just on. But it’s still sampling one state at a time, and whichever one it lands on more often wins the moment. My wife heard me say the first part and pushed back. “Okay, I believe you. But when I’m scared, or hurting, how do I actually get from anxious to grateful? Just deciding to be grateful doesn’t work.” Lisa's pushback to this neuroscience fact I've been teaching for years made me realize that I needed to provide a more tactical solution instead of a simple sound bite like, "Just be grateful and you'll feel less anxious."  I needed to step up, drop the clichés, and give her- and you-  some strategy, because she’s right.   Almost every influencer and self-help guru on the Internet who talks about gratitude skips that exact question. And all of us, including me, need to know what to do when we're feeling so anxious that we can't seem to move in our own lives. Here’s what’s actually happening in your brain:  Anxiety and gratitude are two hands reaching for the same switch in your brain. Whichever one grabs it first is the one that runs the show. So gratitude isn’t a mood you wait to feel your way into. It’s a deliberate redirect you force, on purpose, while the fear is still standing right there in the room with you. title: July 4 always takes me back to Iraq. Here, I'm flying from Qatar to I...
description: July 4 always takes me back to Iraq. Here, I'm flying from Qatar to Iraq. A 34-year-old neurosurgeon. Scared to death. Unsure what I'd face, if I was strong enough to handle it. Wondering if my training was adequate. Whether I'd survive. I'd never carried a gun into surgery before. Never been mortared or rocketed. Never had to triage between 20 different people who were all going to die without urgent care. It was our responsibility to decide who had the best chance and make a quick decision of who went to surgery first- knowing some of them would die waiting. A lot of responsibility, and I didn't know if I could live with the decisions I'd have to make. Some nights, I still ask myself that question. We had to learn on the fly- how to operate while being in danger ourselves, to be prepared not to react to explosions or gunfire, to be able to hand a case off to someone less trained for it if another person came in who needed us more urgently. Commonly had to help general or ortho surgeons when they were needed elsewhere, and they helped me. "Work on this guy while I stabilize that other soldier," was a daily experience. We got used to operating for 24 hours in a row. To multiple sleepless days and nights, to running out of supplies or equipment but never out of patients, and having to improvise.  All for the cause of freedom. The politicians sent us there, and it wasn't our job to debate the whys. Just to save lives- American, coalition, Iraqi civilian, and even terrorists and insurgents. So that's what we did. Fix the person in front of us without judgment or hesitation. It's the only way we could live with ourselves. Do the best for everyone every time. Almost every patient had multiple injuries, and it was common to have 3-5 different procedures happening on a given patient simultaneously. This almost never happens stateside. Five months later. Coming home. I wasn't scared anymore. But I just as many questions; was I strong enough to survive what was already unfolding in my mind and heart?  Those questions took me years to answer.  Every veteran has their own version of them. And that's what the cost of freedom is. Some people give their lives for it, but all of us give parts of our lives to it. Don't take it for granted.  America sends its sons and daughters to these places for the sake of freedom. I'm grateful to have gone and been blessed enough to come home. I think about it every day, 21 years later. My wife and kids have lived it with me. And I think (and dream) of the ones who didn't come home, and those of us who are still trying to. That's what today means to me. To learn more about the war and my journey home, check out my book "No Place to Hide," at my website drleewarren.com #4thofjuly #america250 #iraqwar #veteran

title: After my son Mitch died in 2013, I was stuck. Lisa and I were trying ...
description: After my son Mitch died in 2013, I was stuck. Lisa and I were trying to find our way back to hope, and the two worlds I lived in seemed further apart than ever: science and faith. My training and upbringing as a scientist and surgeon had taught me that trauma and tragedy had the inherent power to wreck us in a variety of ways, and the prevailing neuroscience of the time was that our brains lack the ability to heal and change. We were largely, science said, the product of our genes, upbringing, and experiences. But my faith told a different story. Adversity produces hope, the Bible said. We grow in the face of our trials, and we have a Healer who wants to come alongside us and help us in our times of struggle. We can renew our minds, we can be transformed. So, I felt stuck in a void between the hope of healing, and being in a field full of smart people who taught that you could, at best, manage these moments, but real healing was limited by your neurons and genes. I wrote in my last two books about my experiences that led to finally understanding how science and faith come together, and how my neuroscience training turned out to be incorrect. Ironically, it was science that got me there, in watching the functional imaging research in real time at Auburn University when Lisa and I saw people literally change their brains with their minds. description: Most of us think of our brains as computers, wired to perform in certain ways. The prevailing teaching in neuroscience, and the message to the public from the news, teachers, social media, and most of therapy culture has given you a certain picture of your brain. You’re taught that you have a fancy computer in your skull that creates everything about you- including your personality, potential, and the possibilities for your life- and that brain is you. And that’s all great, as long as the brain lottery gave you a good one, right? Because that teaching (the “You are your brain” idea) implies that you have no control over how your brain came to be how it is or what its potential for change is if it’s not working well for you. If your brain was formed by the genes you inherited from your parents, and shaped by the environment in which you were raised, then it’s really just the luck of the draw if you’re smarter, more resilient, or more capable than someone with a less powerful brain, right? But here’s the problem: You’re living your life with the brain you have, with all its built-in reactions and tendencies and capabilities, and you’ve learned how to operate within those limitations.  And then it happens. You’re maxed out, running through life as best you can and suddenly The Massive Thing (TMT) comes out of nowhere. You were processing and coping and dealing with your family and your wins and losses and finances and fears, and the phone rings, like mine did on the night of August 20, 2013. If you want to know how my family and I found hope again, check out this week's letter. In this post, I dive into the neuroscience of hope and how activating it can literally change your brain, your outlook, and your future. This isn’t fluff. It’s real, it’s practical, and it might just be the thing you need today. 🙏💥 ➡️ Check it out at drleewarren.substack.com! This is the end organ of how thoughts become things, and learning to biopsy your thinking, or take every thought captive as the Bible put it, allows us to then begin to filter out the things that are more or less important in our mission of becoming healthier, feeling better, and being happier. title: 🧠Upstream from every decision and reaction we make in response to the...
description: 🧠Upstream from every decision and reaction we make in response to the thoughts, emotions, and circumstances we have, there is a river of factors like genetics, epigenetic starting points, upbringing, and prior trauma/tragedy/etc.  🧠These things flow into our minds and instantly color things we think about NOW, but they blend so seamlessly into our consciousness that, unless we are careful to examine them (II Corinthians 10:5), they will feel like they are a part of what’s happening in the current situation. 🧠 If we react to them as if they’re currently real, then they blend into our reality and flow downstream, mixing into the rest of our lives and soaking into the lives of everyone we interact with.  ✝️🧠❤️ If we learn to biopsy our thoughts and feelings, we can take action on what we experience as it is, and understand that what’s happened in the past can refine us (Isaiah 48:10), but if doesn’t have to DEFINE us.  🧠 The neuroscience works in our favor here: your brain is designed to heal, and the healing starts with renewing our minds (Romans 12:2).  🧠 Love your downstream life more than you’re drowned by what came before. You can change! You can be healed! You’re not stuck. #selfbrainsurgery

title: Life is often hard, and the traumas, tragedies, dramas, and other mas...
description: Life is often hard, and the traumas, tragedies, dramas, and other massive things we experience can lead us to feeling stuck or hopeless. Also, many of us have been taught to believe that our lives are largely determined by our genetics, our upbringing, or our past experiences. We have accepted the idea that we are really just our brains, and that certain things can happen to wound us in ways from which we cannot recover. But I have very good news for you!  🧠 Modern neuroscience and quantum physics validate what scripture said all along: you are NOT just your brain! Your mind and your brain are not the same thing. 🧠 You are not a computer, you are the programmer. You’re not stuck being a patient, hoping that some therapist or doctor can make things better for you. You, my friend, are the surgeon! Self-brain surgery is what I call the smashing together of scripture, faith, and neuroplasticity, and it puts YOU in charge of your brain. 🧠 Functional brain imaging has now shown conclusively the changing what you think about makes instant, powerful, and widespread structural changes throughout your brain. Your brain literally changes every second of every day of your life, and the primary driving force behind that change is your thinking! That means you are literally performing surgery on your own brain with every thought you think. 🧠 The problem is, if you DON’T actively take control of your thinking, then you simply perpetually rewire your brain in the same way it has performed in the past. In other words, you get better at what you’re doing, even if what you’ve been doing is thinking that your brain was stuck. If you decide to “unstick” your brain, you will begin immediately to see positive change. ✝️ This is why the Bible told us in II Corinthians 10:5 to take every thought captive. Because literally every thought creates something in your brain, to help you or to keep you stuck. Philippians chapter 4 is the textbook of self brain surgery: we learn that gratitude, defeats, anxiety, and that prayer produces peace of mind. 🧠✝️ This is where science and faith smash together! #selfbrainsurgery
